General Abdollahi made the remarks after reviewing the managerial experience and professional background of Akhlaghi, who met with the top military commander on Saturday to discuss requirements for strengthening defense capabilities and enhancing logistical support for the Armed Forces.
​
Highlighting the critical and sensitive nature of the Ministry of Defense’s mission to meet the needs of the Armed Forces, Gen. Abdollahi described Akhlaghi as well-qualified for the cabinet post, saying his experience meets the ministry's current conditions and requirements.
​
The top commander also emphasized the need to leverage domestic capacity for defense equipment and weaponry and to strengthen industrial infrastructure to enhance defense capabilities.
​
Pointing to the Ministry of Defense's strategic role in maintaining and enhancing the readiness of the Armed Forces, Abdollahi stressed the need for cohesive management, meticulous planning and optimal use of domestic expertise.
​
Akhlaghi, for his part, underscored the importance of sustained, effective support for the Armed Forces, highlighting several key priorities for the Ministry of Defense, including maintaining supply chain stability, producing defense equipment, advancing technological capabilities and strengthening welfare support for personnel.
​
President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Akhlaghi — a senior official at the Ministry of Defense and former head of the Aerospace Industries Organization — to serve as the country's Minister of Defense, submitting his name to Parliament for a vote of confidence scheduled for October 18.

JOHN BRENNAN JUST LOST A MAJOR COURT BATTLE — AND THE TIMING IS INTERESTING.

As we’ve been tracking for months, the DOJ’s Florida-based “grand conspiracy” investigation continues to move forward, examining the origins of Russiagate and the investigations targeting President Trump.

Now another significant development.

On October 15, federal Judge Jia Cobb dismissed former CIA Director John Brennan’s lawsuit seeking to force the DOJ to preserve records related to its investigation.

Brennan argued that records could potentially be destroyed or withheld, compromising his ability to defend himself against possible future prosecution.

The judge rejected his case for lack of standing, finding that Brennan had not demonstrated an imminent risk of records being destroyed or a concrete injury warranting court intervention.

But here’s where the timing becomes interesting.

October 15 was ALSO the date Brennan had originally been scheduled to appear before the federal grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida.

That appearance has now reportedly been POSTPONED.

Remember, Brennan is one of several former intelligence and law enforcement officials identified in reporting about the expanding investigation, which has reportedly examined both the origins of Russiagate and the subsequent investigations of Donald Trump.

We’ve also tracked the growing number of subpoenas, discussions of potential witness immunity, and the DOJ’s efforts to obtain testimony from FBI personnel involved in the Mar-a-Lago investigation.

My theory remains that these seemingly separate developments may be pieces of a much larger legal strategy.

The key questions now:

Will Brennan ultimately testify before the grand jury? Will additional witnesses cooperate? And will prosecutors be able to establish evidence of an actual criminal conspiracy?

The investigation remains active, the legal maneuvering continues, and Brennan’s next grand-jury appearance is one to watch.
